newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea set to increase food aid to North Korea.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea set to increase food aid to North Korea.

text.p: South Korea, trying to coax Pyongyang into peace talks, was set on Wednesday to increase food aid to help North Korea stave off famine.
North Korea's food crisis was underscored by news on Tuesday that the Stalinist state had told international aid agencies 134 children had died of malnutrition.
"We are favourably considering the latest appeal by the World Food Programme (WFP) to increase aid to North Korea," a foreign ministry spokesman said.

A senior government official told Reuters that Seoul had decided to boost its contribution to the U.N. body, which last week raised an appeal to $95.5 million from $41.6 million, enough to buy 200,000 tonnes of food.
"We are still discussing the size of the increase. We will also have to consult with the United States," said the official, who asked not to be identified.
South Korea pledged $6 million to the original WFP appeal and the United States $10 million. On Tuesday Washington said it was considering raising its contribution.
North Korea is preparing its formal response to a joint U.S.-South Korean offer for four-nation peace talks, which would also include China.

"I think our humanitarian gestures will help create a better atmosphere for the talks," the official said. "I expect a favourable response from Pyongyang but I would be surprised if they agreed to the proposal with no strings attached."
A senior government official said Pyongyang may demand closer ties with the United States.
"I think the North will seek guarantees for improved ties with Washington," said the official, who declined to be identified.

He said when the United States and South Korea briefed North Korth Korea over the talks proposal last month in New York, Pyongyang's vice foreign minister Kim Gye-gwan had pointed out "inequalities" among participants.

China, which fought alongside North Korea in the 1950-53 Korean War, has diplomatic and flourishing business ties with South Korea, while Seoul's ally Washington maintains economic sanctions against North Korea.
Pyongyang has been demanding food aid in return for an agreement to take part in the talks aimed at securing a peace treaty to replace a truce that ended the Korean War.
Washington and South Korea maintain substantial food aid could be discussed during the talks.

In addition to the WFP's relief aid, U.S. grains giant Cargill Inc has struck a deal to barter about 20,000 tonnes of wheat for about 4,000 tonnes of zinc, and private groups in South Korea plan to raise about $20 million to ship 110,000 tonnes of corn to North Korea.

Kim Hak-joon, a former presidential policy advisor, said he expected North Korea to join the peace talks because it wanted to end the food crisis to pave the way for a formal accession of its leader Kim Jong-il this year.
"The North is now desperate for food and the seriousness of the problem would force it to the peace table," he said.

North Korean officials have said they expect Kim Jong-il to succeed the posts of state president and general secretary of the communist party after the third anniversary of his father Kim Il-sung's death in July.
The posts have been vacant since Kim Il-sung's death.
